title: Could this be luck?
objectives: Frame a claim as a null and an alternative hypothesis.

screens.title: Fourteen out of twenty
screens.prose: A trader shows you her last 20 trades: 14 winners and 6 losers. She says she has an edge. Suppose instead that each trade is a fair coin flip.
screens.question: With no edge at all, how often would 20 trades give 14 or more winners?

options.text: Almost never: less than 1 time in 1,000
options.why: You judged 14 of 20 as if it were 14 in a row. Luck can reach exactly 14 wins in 38,760 different orders.
That is nearer the chance of 12 or more wins, 0.25. Each extra win beyond 12 makes luck much rarer.
More than half of seasons reach 10, the average. But 14 sits four wins further out.

hints.text: Ten wins is the most likely count for a coin. How far out is 14?
Her 14 winners are four more than a coin’s average of 10.
The exact chance is $P(W \ge 14) = 0.0577$, where $W$ counts the wins in 20 fair trades.

feedback.correct: Luck alone does it about one season in 17.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Picture many traders with no edge, each making 20 trades.

explain.text: With a fair coin, 14 or more wins in 20 has chance 0.0577, about one season in 17. That is unusual, but far from impossible. The next screen checks it by simulation.

screens.title: Seasons of luck
screens.prose: Each run plays seasons of 20 fair trades and counts the wins. The bars show the share of seasons at each count, and the dashed lines the exact chances. The 14-or-more bars are coloured.

derive.caption: {{(ran).toLocaleString('en-GB')}} seasons. Share with 14 or more wins: {{fixed(total(['x14', 'x15', 'x16', 'x17', 'x18', 'x19', 'x20']), 3)}}

screens.question: Run at least 1,000 seasons. What share of them reached 14 or more wins?

widget.label: Share of seasons with 14 or more wins
widget.accept: any value from 0.043 to 0.073. The exact share is $P(W \ge 14) = 0.0577$.

hints.text: Press Run 1,000 and read the caption under the chart.
Only the coloured bars count: 14 wins and more.
The caption adds up the coloured bars for you.

feedback.correct: Close to 0.058: a coin-flip trader gets there about one season in 17.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run 1,000 seasons and read the share in the caption.

byKey.one-bar: You read the 14 bar alone. Seasons with 15, 16 or more wins count too.
byKey.rest: That is the share with 13 or fewer wins. You want the coloured bars.
byKey.percent: Give the share as a decimal: 5.8% is 0.058.

explain.text: Your 1,000 seasons gave about 57 with 14 or more wins. As the runs grow, the share settles on the exact value $P(W \ge 14) = 0.0577$. So luck alone matches her record about one season in 17.

screens.title: Naming the two stories
screens.prose: You assumed there was no edge, then asked how surprising 14 wins would be. That assumption is the **null hypothesis** $H_0$. The claim tested against it is the **alternative hypothesis** $H_1$. Both are statements about $p$, her true chance of winning a trade.
screens.question: Which pair frames her claim?

options.why: You put her claim in the null. The null is the dull story, no edge, which the data must embarrass.
You used $14/20 = 0.7$, the win rate in the data. Hypotheses are fixed before the data are seen.

options.text: $H_0$: the 14 wins were luck; $H_1$: they were skill
options.why: You wrote the hypotheses about the 14 wins seen. They are about $p$, the true chance behind every trade.

hints.text: Which hypothesis lets you draw a chart of wins?
Only one value of $p$ gives the chart on screen.
Put the dull story, $p = 0.5$, in $H_0$. Put her claim in $H_1$.

feedback.correct: No edge is the null; her claim, $p > 0.5$, is the alternative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The null fixes $p$ at the no-edge value; the alternative is her claim.

explain.text: The null pins $p$ to 0.5, so we can draw this chart. Her claim, $p > 0.5$, is the alternative. The test asks how surprising 14 wins would be under $H_0$: chance 0.0577.

screens.title: Both directions
screens.prose: A risk manager asks a different question: is her win rate different from 0.5, in either direction? Then 6 wins would worry him as much as 14. This is a **two-sided** alternative, $H_1: p \ne 0.5$. Her claim, $p > 0.5$, was **one-sided**.
screens.question: Tap every win count at least as far from 10 as 14 is.

hints.text: How far is 14 from 10? Which counts below 10 are just as far?
6 and 14 are both four wins from 10.
Tap 0 to 6 and 14 to 20: fourteen bars in all.

feedback.correct: Both tails: 6 or fewer, and 14 or more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap the counts four or more wins from 10, on both sides.

byKey.one-tail: You tapped only the top tail. Under $p \ne 0.5$, 6 wins or fewer is just as far from 10.
byKey.x7: 7 wins is three from 10, closer than 14 is. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.
byKey.x8: 8 wins is 2 from 10, closer than 14 is. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.
byKey.x9: 9 wins is 1 from 10, closer than 14 is. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.
byKey.x10: 10 wins is the centre itself. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.
byKey.x11: 11 wins is 1 from 10, closer than 14 is. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.
byKey.x12: 12 wins is 2 from 10, closer than 14 is. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.
byKey.x13: 13 wins is three from 10, closer than 14 is. Tap only counts at least four wins from 10.

explain.text: You tapped both tails: 6 wins or fewer, and 14 or more. Each is at least four wins from 10. A two-sided test counts both as extreme as 14.

screens.title: The two-sided chance
screens.prose: The chart is symmetric about 10, because a fair trade wins and loses with equal chance. So $P(W \le 6) = P(W \ge 14) = 0.0577$.

state.caption: Coloured: at least four wins from 10

screens.question: Under $H_0$, what is the chance of a result at least as far from 10 as 14 wins?

hints.text: Which coloured tails count now?
Both tails count, and they are mirror images.
Add the two tails: $0.0577 + 0.0577$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the chances of both coloured tails.

byKey.one-tail: That is the top tail alone. The two-sided question counts 6 or fewer wins too.
byKey.half: You halved the tail. Two-sided adds the other tail, so the chance grows.
byKey.inside: That is the chance of landing between 7 and 13. You want the two tails.

explain.text: Both tails count, so the chance is $0.0577 + 0.0577 = 0.1153$. The same 14 wins look twice as ordinary under the two-sided question. That is why the side is chosen before the data are seen.

screens.title: A perfect fit
screens.prose: A third trader wins exactly 10 of 20, the most likely count if $p = 0.5$. The data could hardly fit $H_0$ better.

state.caption: Her 10 wins sit at the peak: $P(W \ge 10) = 0.588$

screens.question: What does her record show about $H_0: p = 0.5$?

options.text: No evidence against $H_0$, but it does not show that $p$ is exactly 0.5
It proves she has no edge
options.why: You read a perfect fit as proof. A trader with $p = 0.55$ also reaches 10 or more wins three times in four.

options.text: It is evidence she is worse than a coin
options.why: Ten wins is the centre of the null chart, not its low tail.

options.text: The test cannot be used on a result at the centre
options.why: It can: $P(W \ge 10) = 0.588$. The answer is simply that 10 wins is not surprising.

hints.text: Would a trader with a small edge, say $p = 0.55$, often win 10 of 20?
Her count sits at the peak of the null chart.
A test can find evidence against $H_0$. It cannot show $H_0$ is true.

feedback.correct: Fitting the null is not proving it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a small edge could also produce 10 wins.

explain.text: Under $H_0$, 10 or more wins has chance 0.588, so nothing here is surprising. But $p = 0.55$ gives 10 or more wins with chance 0.751, so it fits too. A test finds evidence against $H_0$; it never proves $H_0$.

screens.title: The wrong way round
screens.prose: A colleague sets up the test the other way round. $H_0$: she has an edge, $p > 0.5$. $H_1$: no edge, $p = 0.5$. He says 14 wins fit $H_0$ well, so the test supports her.

state.caption: This chart needs one value of $p$. “$p > 0.5$” gives no single chart.

screens.question: What is wrong with his set-up?

options.text: $H_0$ must fix $p$ at one value so that surprise can be measured. Her claim belongs in $H_1$.
Nothing: either way round gives the same answer
options.why: You swapped the roles. A test can only reject $H_0$, so with her claim there the best it can say is “not rejected”.

options.text: The null should be $p = 0.7$, her win rate in these trades
options.why: You took the null from the data being tested. Data always fit a null built from themselves.
That asks whether she is worse than a coin. Her claim is that she is better.

hints.text: Which value of $p$ would you use to draw the chart under his $H_0$?
This chart exists only because $p$ is fixed at 0.5.
A null must name one value. The claim we hope to show goes in $H_1$.

feedback.correct: The dull story goes in $H_0$; the claim goes in $H_1$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which hypothesis the test can reject, and which one fixes $p$.

byKey.same: You swapped the roles. A test can only reject $H_0$, so with her claim there the best it can say is “not rejected”.
byKey.data: You took the null from the data being tested. Data always fit a null built from themselves.

explain.text: Under “$p > 0.5$” there is no single chart, so no chance can be computed. Worse, failing to reject a null is not support for it. Put the dull story in $H_0$ and see whether the data embarrass it.

screens.title: Setting up any test
screens.prose: Each time you did three things. State $H_0$, which fixes one value: $p = p_0$. State $H_1$, the claim: one-sided, $p > p_0$ or $p < p_0$, or two-sided, $p \ne p_0$. Then ask how often luck alone gives data this extreme: $$P(\text{data at least as extreme as seen} \mid H_0).$$
screens.question: Which of these can serve as a null hypothesis for a win rate?

options.why: You chose a range of values. A range gives no single chart to measure surprise against.
You chose $\hat p$, which is computed from the data. A hypothesis is about the true $p$.
You wrote a chance that a hypothesis is true. A hypothesis is a statement about $p$ itself.

feedback.correct: One fixed value of the true $p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A null names one value of the true parameter.

screens.title: Three desk claims
screens.prose: Three claims reach the research meeting. Frame each one as a test: a null and an alternative. Two cards are spare.

rows: This value factor earns a premium
This change to the algorithm improved fill rates
The two desks' daily P&L differ

screens.question: Place a null and an alternative for each claim.

hints.text: Each null says nothing is going on: no premium, no change, no difference.
Read the verbs: “earns”, “improved” and “differ”. Which name a direction?
Factor: $\mu = 0$ against $\mu > 0$. Fills: $f = 0.60$ against $f > 0.60$. Desks: $\mu_A = \mu_B$ against $\mu_A \ne \mu_B$.

feedback.correct: Three dull nulls, and the claims as alternatives.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each null is “nothing is going on”; each alternative is the claim.

byKey.xd: “Differ” names no direction. Use $\mu_A \ne \mu_B$ unless you said in advance which desk should be higher.
byKey.xr: The claim is that fills improved, which is a direction. Use $f > 0.60$.
byKey.f1: A premium is the claim, so $\mu > 0$ goes in $H_1$. The null is no premium, $\mu = 0$.
byKey.r1: An improvement is the claim, so $f > 0.60$ goes in $H_1$. The null is no change, $f = 0.60$.
byKey.d1: A difference is the claim, so $\mu_A \ne \mu_B$ goes in $H_1$. The null is no difference.

explain.text: Each null is the dull story: no premium, no change, no difference. “Earns” and “improved” name a direction, so those tests are one-sided. “Differ” does not, so the desks get $\mu_A \ne \mu_B$.

ideas: The null hypothesis $H_0$ is the dull story, such as no edge: $p = 0.5$. The claim goes in the alternative $H_1$.
A test asks how often luck alone gives data at least as extreme as yours. Fourteen or more wins in 20 fair trades has chance 0.0577.
A one-sided $H_1$, such as $p > 0.5$, counts one tail. A two-sided $H_1$, $p \ne 0.5$, counts both. Choose before you see the data.

formula.name: Fourteen or more wins by luck
formula.note: Count every result at least as extreme as the one seen.

summary.trap: The claim never goes in $H_0$, and a test never proves $H_0$. Data that fit the null are only no evidence against it.

quiz.prose: A signal calls the next day’s direction correctly on 58 of 100 days. You want to know whether it beats a coin.
quiz.question: Which pair of hypotheses fits?

options.why: You built the null from the 58 days seen. The null is the no-skill value, 0.5.
You put the claim in the null. The claim goes in $H_1$.
That alternative says the signal is worse than a coin. The claim is that it is better.

feedback.correct: No skill is the null; beating a coin is the alternative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix the null at the no-skill value.

explain.text: A coin calls direction with chance 0.5, so $H_0: p = 0.5$. “Beats a coin” names a direction, so $H_1: p > 0.5$. The 0.58 is the estimate the test will judge.

quiz.prose: A risk model should be breached on 5% of days. Too many breaches means it understates risk; too few means it overstates risk.
quiz.question: Which alternative fits a check of the model?

options.why: You counted only too many breaches. Too few is also a failure here.
That is the null: the model is right.
You counted only too few breaches. Too many is also a failure here.

feedback.correct: Either direction is a failure, so the test is two-sided.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which breach rates would count against the model.

explain.text: The model fails if breaches are too frequent or too rare. So the alternative is two-sided, $p \ne 0.05$, against $H_0: p = 0.05$.

quiz.prose: Under $H_0: p = 0.5$ for 20 trades, $P(W \ge 14) = 0.0577$. Another trader won only 6 of 20, and you test $H_1: p < 0.5$.
quiz.question: What is $P(W \le 6)$ under $H_0$?

widget.label: Chance of 6 or fewer wins
widget.accept: 0.0577, by symmetry with 14 or more wins (± 0.0005)

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Under $p = 0.5$ the chart is a mirror image about 10.

byKey.complement: That is the chance of 7 or more wins. You want 6 or fewer.
byKey.both: That adds both tails. The alternative $p < 0.5$ counts only the low tail.

explain.text: With $p = 0.5$, winning $k$ trades is as likely as losing $k$. So 6 or fewer wins mirrors 14 or more: $P(W \le 6) = 0.0577$.

quiz.prose: A test of $H_0$: “no edge” gives a result in the middle of the null chart. A colleague writes: “We have shown the strategy has no edge.”
quiz.question: Which correction is right?

options.text: We found no evidence of an edge; a small edge could still exist
The statement is fine: a central result proves $H_0$
options.why: You treated a good fit as proof. A small edge would give a central result often too.

options.text: We should now make “edge” the null and test again
options.why: You moved the claim into the null. A test can never support its own null.

options.text: The result shows the strategy loses money
options.why: A central result says nothing about losses. It is simply unsurprising under no edge.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether a small edge could have produced the same result.

explain.text: A result in the middle of the null chart is no evidence against $H_0$. A strategy with a small edge produces such results often too. So the honest line is “no evidence of an edge”.
